deathBook.name: The DeathBook
rules: The reader whose name is written in this notebook shall never leave the Library.
The notebook takes effect only if the writer has seen the reader's face. The mirror of a vestibule will do.
A written name cannot be erased. A copy already exists, one letter apart, in another hexagon.
There is no use looking for the way out in the books: all of them describe it, none of them contains it.
Every name written here is that of a reader the Library has kept.
The notebook never runs out of pages. There is always one left for the next name.
If the circumstances are written after the name, they shall come to pass.
circumstances: hexagon 4021, while reading
on the stairs, between two galleries
at the foot of a shelf, a book open over the face
searching for the catalogue of catalogues
before the mirror of the vestibule
at the end of an unlit gallery
counting the books on the fifth shelf
on the last page
leaning over the railing, without falling
copying out a page that made no sense
closing a book too soon
on the landing, not knowing whether going up or down
in the air shaft, between two floors
looking for a book about oneself
after reading the same page a thousand times
by the light of the last lamp
waiting for someone who never came
deciphering a line that made sense
in the closet, standing, to sleep
in the middle of a sentence
putting a book back in its place
without finding what was sought
believing what was sought had been found
the day the counting of hexagons stopped
between two books identical but for a comma
writing one's own name
listening to footsteps, overhead
following a gallery that turned back on itself
after the thousandth crossing
scenario: {name} takes a book from the Library.
Reads it to the last page.
The last page closes nothing: it opens a door.
Takes another. Then another. Then another still.
The end of a book is only the threshold of the next.
And every beginning promises an end it does not always keep.

oriana.name: The Biography of Oriana
oriana.subtitle: One Block at a Time
quotes: “She explained blockchain to me between Lisbon and Madrid.”
“She closed the bar, then explained blockchain to me.”
oriana.blurb: Developer, traveller, queen of late nights and apostle of the blockchain: Oriana has a story to tell. Several, actually. All at once. From her first word to the suitcase packed for America, the life of a woman who never kept it short, told by a biographer who tried.
copyright: © Oriana. All rights reserved, all blocks validated.
in the writing of this book.
Excessive anecdotes may harm the health
of those around you. Read responsibly.
dedication: who listened to me talk about blockchain

chapters.label: Chapter 1
chapters.title: The First Word
opening: Oriana’s first word was not “mummy”. Nor “daddy”. According to her mother, it was a full sentence, with a subordinate clause, spoken at eleven months to a baker who hadn’t asked for anything.¹ She hasn’t really stopped for breath since.
At school, her reports all said the same thing, in different handwriting: “Brilliant pupil. Talkative.” One maths teacher once added: “Very talkative. But she’s right.” She had it framed.
This book tells her life. It could have been shorter. She asked to proofread it.
chapters.note: It was a question. And the baker answered.

chapters.label: Chapter 2
chapters.title: Developer
opening: Oriana became a developer by accident, one evening when she was explaining to a friend why his website didn’t work. By midnight, the website worked. By one, the friend was asleep. She was still talking.¹

At work, she is one of those people who ask questions in meetings, then answer them. “Any questions? — No. — I’ll answer anyway.” Her colleagues find her brilliant, funny and sometimes a little tiring, but always in that order.
She codes fast and well, with music on and a cup of tea going cold. Her commit messages are short. It is, by general agreement, the only short thing about her.
chapters.note: He wasn’t asleep, he was thinking. I checked by asking him the question again the next day.

chapters.label: Chapter 3
chapters.title: The Revelation
opening: She discovered blockchain on a Tuesday, in an article nobody had recommended. By the end of the first page, she understood. By the end of the second, she was convinced. By the end of the third, she was already explaining it to the colleague at the next desk, who was on the phone.¹

A ledger nobody can erase, where every block remembers the one before: for someone who never forgets anything anyone has told her, it was almost obvious. That evening she told anyone who would listen: “It’s me, as a technology.”
Nobody argued. Nobody argues with Oriana for very long.
chapters.note: He hung up. So he was interested.

chapters.label: Chapter 4
chapters.title: The Gospel
opening: Ever since, she has been explaining blockchain. To her colleagues, her family, the baker, the bus driver, strangers on a night train who hadn’t asked for anything and who, by morning, knew what proof of stake is.¹
She has a short version, twenty minutes long, and a long version nobody has ever heard in full. She always starts with: “Picture a big notebook.” You never know when she’ll stop. Neither does she.
Rumour has it that the baker eventually bought a token. She refuses to talk about it. Oriana talks about it a lot.
chapters.note: “Who hadn’t asked for anything”: that’s the biographer talking. I saw their eyes. They were asking.

chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: Around the World
opening: Oriana took her first plane at nineteen. By landing, she knew the first names, jobs and holiday plans of both her neighbours in the row, and the flight attendant’s too.¹ Since then, she has never really travelled alone: there is always someone next to her, and they always end up listening.

Lisbon, Tokyo, Reykjavik, Marrakech: she collects stamps in her passport and conversations in taxis. They say a driver in Lisbon went round the city twice just to hear the end of her explanation of proof of work.
She comes back from every trip with too many photos, too many stories and not enough time to tell them all. She tries anyway. The notebook that follows gives an idea, in shorter form.
chapters.note: And the pilot’s. He came to say hello at the end; we talked for half an hour on the jet bridge.

chapters.label: Chapter 6
chapters.title: Last Orders
opening: Oriana loves parties. The long ones, the ones that start with “just one drink” and end when the bar closes, or a little after. She is always the last to leave, because there is always someone she hasn’t talked to yet.¹

At three in the morning, you’ll usually find her by the decks, explaining blockchain to the DJ. He nods along to the beat. She takes it as a yes. The mornings after are hard, but her memories are intact: she can tell you who said what, and at what time.
Nobody remembers how those nights end. The blockchain does. So does Oriana.
chapters.note: I wasn’t drunk, I was enthusiastic.

chapters.label: Chapter 7
chapters.title: The Five-Minute Meeting
opening: The meeting was meant to last five minutes. It said so in the invitation, in bold: “quick sync”. Oriana had just one remark. She raised her hand at 10:01.¹

By 10:20, she had reached the remark, or at least its background. By 10:40, she had answered three questions nobody had asked. At 11:00, someone opened the window. At 11:02, she concluded: “Anyway, that’s all.” It was not all.
Since then, the team always books an hour for quick syncs. They often finish early. Except when Oriana has a remark.
chapters.note: The remark was important, and so was the rest. Besides, nobody left. Well, one colleague, but he had a train to catch. I sent him the end in writing. Four pages. He thanked me. Well, he gave it a thumbs-up.

chapters.label: Chapter 8
chapters.title: The Cat on the Keyboard
opening: Oriana has cats. They listen to her talk about blockchain without ever interrupting, which makes them, in her opinion, the best colleagues she has ever had.¹

One of them likes to sleep on her keyboard. One day, it pushed a commit: “ggggggggggggggg”. AlexH, her colleague, reviewed it with the utmost seriousness. He left a single comment: “Rename.” Oriana defended the cat for twenty minutes. The commit is still there.
This is the shortest chapter in the book. She found it too short. The cat said nothing.
chapters.note: That’s also why I talk to them so much. Somebody has to talk in this house. They have opinions, mind you, but they keep them to themselves, which I respect, even if I don’t understand it.

chapters.label: Chapter 9
chapters.title: America
opening: Oriana dreams of living in the United States. She talks about it often, mostly New York, sometimes Austin, once Seattle “for the rain”. She has even started her visa application. It is almost ready.¹

She has it all planned: the apartment with a view, the corner café where she’ll know everyone within a week, and the first American she’ll explain blockchain to. He doesn’t know it yet. He has a few months of peace left.
The suitcase is half packed, in a corner of the bedroom. The cat sleeps in it.
chapters.note: “Almost” meaning two documents are missing, well, three, and an ID photo where I’m not talking, which is harder than you’d think: the photographer tried four times, the fifth was the one but my eyes were closed, he said it would do, I don’t think so, nor does the embassy, so I’m going back on Tuesday.

chapters.title: Epilogue: Anyway
opening: This book ends here. Oriana doesn’t. As you read these lines, she is surely telling someone something, in great detail, with a parenthesis that will never close.¹

One day, she will move to the other side of the ocean. She will look at the city from her window, coffee in hand, and call the friends she left behind to tell them everything. The call will be long. They will pick up anyway.
She said she’d keep it short. She said “anyway”. We believe her.

notes: That’s not quite it.
Three times, not two.
I’m adding this because the biographer won’t.
It was a Tuesday, not a Wednesday. I remember: on Tuesdays there are croissants.
The biographer wasn’t there. I was.
I have a photo, if needed.
He forgets to mention I was right.
Which reminds me of a story, in Tokyo, with a man singing karaoke.
I’ll come back to this, it’s important.
It should also be said that blockchain solves this problem, but I’ll explain later. Or now, while we’re at it.
Picture a big notebook.
To be honest, it was more like four in the morning.
I would have written this paragraph differently. Longer, but clearer.
My cat disagrees, but he doesn’t get a chapter. Well, he does: chapter eight.
Speaking of which, the visa application is moving. Slowly, but it’s moving.
I was asked to keep it short. I’m keeping it short.
This is a parenthesis (containing another (and a third, which I’ll close later)).
And it wasn’t proof of work, it was proof of stake.
The Lisbon taxi driver is called Rui, by the way. He still sends me messages. Well, I send him messages, and he reads them.
AlexH says this note is too long. AlexH says that about everything.
oriana.longLine: She has long dreamt of living in the United States.¹
oriana.longNote: “Long” is a figure of speech, we should be precise: since 2009 exactly, since a documentary about San Francisco I watched at my aunt’s, the one with the ginger cat, not the other one. Besides, it isn’t a dream, it’s a plan, and a plan isn’t a dream because it has steps. Step one: the application. The application is almost ready, only two documents missing, well, three, and a photo where I’m not talking. Step two: choose the city. New York for the energy, Austin for tech, Seattle for the rain that will remind me of home, but not too much. Step three: explain blockchain to the Americans, who already know it, but badly, and that’s where I come in. Step four: find a bar where they know my name before the end of the first night, which, between us, shouldn’t take long. So I was saying the biographer should have written “since 2009”, but he didn’t let me finish, which, between us, is a first, and I fully intend to bring it up in the epilogue, unless he cuts that too, in which case
oriana.longNoteRest: (continued from p. 311) … in which case I’ll write it in the margins, or in a second book, or both. There. That’s all. For now.
captions: Lisbon: Rui, taxi driver, three laps of the city. He got proof of stake on the third.
Tokyo: the karaoke man wanted to sing. I explained smart contracts to him, he sang afterwards.
Reykjavik: northern lights at 2 a.m. I talked through the whole aurora. The others say it was beautiful.
Marrakech: three hours haggling over a rug. I didn’t want a rug, I wanted to chat.
Montreal: party until 5 a.m. The bartender now knows blockchain and my name. Mostly my name.
The next page. I’m saving the spot.
oriana.journalIntro: Oriana writes everything down. Since she discovered blockchain, she writes it in blocks: each block keeps the fingerprint of the one before, and nothing is ever erased. Here are the latest. There are more.
oriana.thanks: Thank you to everyone who listened to me: my colleagues, my friends, my cats, Rui, the DJ in Montreal, the karaoke man and the United States embassy, which will listen to me soon. Thank you to AlexH, who proofread this book and requested changes on every footnote. Thank you to the biographer, who did his best to cut me off and almost never managed. And thank you, reader: if you want to know more, come and see me. I have time.
also: Why You Should Care About Blockchain (volumes 1 to 7)
colophon: on the presses of the Library of Babel.

alexH.name: AlexH, My Code, My PR
quotes: “Finally, a flawless book: he reviewed himself.”
alexH.blurb: From the first “Hello, world” to his ten-thousandth change request, the life of a lead dev who lets nothing slide: not a variable name, not a comma, not a line too long. The bugs got through anyway.
copyright: No tests were harmed in the writing of this book.
The bugs described are real; any resemblance to
dedication: the only one stricter than me.

chapters.title: Prologue
opening: It all starts with a comma. The one missing, one morning, from a sticky note on the office fridge: “Milk, coffee sugar”. He added it in pen, between “coffee” and “sugar”, without a word to anyone. Nobody had asked him to. Nobody thanked him.

That was his first review. Ten thousand more would follow, all just as precise, all just as unsolicited. Variable names, lines too long, trailing spaces nobody else could see. He could see them. He still does.
This book tells that life, PR by PR. It has been proofread, of course. Several times. By him. You will not find a single typo in it. As for bugs, we guarantee nothing.

chapters.label: Chapter 1
chapters.title: Hello, World
opening: His first program was one line long. It printed “Hello, world” and worked on the first try, which should have been enough. He rewrote it four times that evening anyway. The quotes were the wrong kind. The indentation was off by one space. And “world”, in his view, deserved an explanation.
The fifth version was eleven lines long. It was commented, typed, filed in a folder with his name on it. It printed “Hello, world” exactly like the first one, but with a clear conscience.

That evening he understood something essential: a program that works is only a draft. A clean program, on the other hand, is a work of art. Whether it works is a detail to be sorted out later, usually in another ticket.

chapters.label: Chapter 2
chapters.title: First Commit
opening: The message of his first commit was three paragraphs long. The first explained why. The second explained how. The third announced what he planned to do next, with a date. He was already following, without knowing it, a convention that did not exist yet.

The code itself was two lines. One fixed a typo in a comment. Nobody ever found out what the other one did. He discovered it six years later, rereading his history one Sunday, for fun. He opened a ticket against himself. He rejected it: the title was badly worded.

Since then he commits often, and always well. Every message starts with an imperative verb. None says “wip”. None says “fix”. There is one, just one, that says “oops”. He claims it wasn’t him. Git blame claims otherwise.

chapters.label: Chapter 3
chapters.title: The Conflict
opening: The conflict came on a Thursday, around 3 pm. Two branches, one file, two worldviews: one indented with tabs, the other with spaces. The whole team gathered around his screen. Some were already talking about a holy war.

He settled it in ten seconds. Spaces, two per level, as it should be. He then reread the file’s four hundred lines, renamed three functions along the way and put the imports back in order. The merge was gorgeous.
The rest of the conflict, something about a dropped database table, waited until Monday. Nobody had noticed. To be fair, the code that dropped it was remarkably well written.

chapters.label: Chapter 4
chapters.title: The Review
opening: To him, a review is not a formality. It is a conversation, long, precise and usually one-way. He reads every line. He comments on every name. He asks why. Then he asks why again, in case the first answer was just an excuse.

Legend has it that a three-line PR once got forty-two comments from him. Not true: there were forty-three, but the last one simply said “thanks”. Those who survived his reviews speak of them with respect, and a slight weariness. All of them write flawless code today.

And when the PR finally goes through, clean as a whistle, sometimes the bug is still in it. But it is well named, properly typed, and documented. Just read the comment above it: “TODO: check this case”. Spelled perfectly.

chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: Friday, 5:59 pm
opening: He had said it, and even written it in the README: no deploys on Fridays. The rule was in bold, with an example and a counterexample. Nobody could claim not to know it.

That Friday, the PR was perfect. Reviewed, formatted, every variable carefully named, not a comma out of place. He had approved it at 5:40 pm, adding: “for Monday”. At 5:59 pm, someone clicked the button. At 6:02 pm, production went down.

He spent the evening putting things right, calmly, without a word of reproach. The error message, at least, was perfectly indented. He pointed it out on Monday morning, in the meeting. It was the only positive thing he said that day.

chapters.label: Chapter 6
chapters.title: Rollback
opening: Going back is not a failure, he likes to say. It is a commit like any other, as long as it is well written. That evening he undid three days of work in a single command, without flinching.

Then he spent an hour on the rollback’s message. It explained what had been done, why it had to be undone, and how to keep it from happening again. The text was so clear, so well structured, that it now hangs in the break room.
The bug, however, never left. It was in another file, one the rollback hadn’t touched. It is still there. But next to it, these days, everything is very clean.

chapters.label: Chapter 7
chapters.title: Refactor
opening: Nobody had asked him for a refactor. He did one anyway, on a Sunday, “just to rename two or three things”. On Monday the PR touched three hundred files. Nothing was called what it used to be.

Everything was clearer. Functions finally said what they did. Folders were sorted logically, then alphabetically. The tests, all three of them, had been renamed too. They all failed, but under perfectly explicit names.
He judged it a good start. The team took two weeks to find their files again. None had been changed, except for their names. To this day, it is the best-named refactor in the project’s history.

chapters.title: Epilogue: LGTM
opening: Today he still reviews. PRs, READMEs, his colleagues’ messages, restaurant menus and road signs. He once wrote to a town hall about a comma. He won.

Only once in his career did he type “LGTM” and nothing else. People still talk about it in hushed voices, by the coffee machine. Some say he was tired. Others that he hadn’t read it. He maintains the code was simply perfect.
This book ends here, but his reviews don’t. If you find a mistake in it, open a ticket: he will read it. If there is a bug, on the other hand, don’t worry. It is surely very well named.

captions: His first review: forty-two comments about naming. The bug got through.
The merge conflict. He resolved it, then renamed the branch.
A Friday, 5:59 pm. The code was spotless. Prod went down anyway.
The rollback. The commit message, at least, followed the convention.
“Just a small refactor.” Three hundred lines renamed, none fixed.
The fix that repaired everything. Rejected: wrong branch name.
A perfectly indented console.log, in production for two years.
The only “LGTM” of his career. There was a bug in it.
alexH.thanks: Thanks to my reviewers, whom I made rename everything that could be renamed, including these acknowledgements. Thanks to the linter, which held firm. Thanks to the bugs, which got through anyway. And thank you, reader: if you find a mistake in this book, open a ticket. If it’s a bug, it’s fine.
also: My Code, My PR, Volume 2 (in review)
colophon: on the day of the merge,
by the presses of the Library of Babel.

back.blurb: The blank page: that moment when the writer, pen raised, can no longer find the first word. Dread, vertigo, silence. After years of research, the author at last delivers, in 410 pages, the complete explanation of this mysterious affliction.
reviews: “You close it just as you opened it.”
